title: The reviewer that said yes
scenario: A studio uses an agent that makes a 30-second tea ad and a second model that reviews it. You judge the rubric and the loop, using the exhibit. The rubrics and the log are made up for this case.
exhibit:
RUBRIC DRAFT 1 (written by the agent, made up for this case)
  - The ad feels premium.
  - The ad is on brand.
  - Overall quality is high.

RUBRIC DRAFT 2 (written by the studio, made up for this case)
  1. The logo is readable in the last 2 seconds.
  2. The only words on screen are the approved tagline: "Steep slowly."
  3. The tea box has the same green lid in every shot where it appears.
  4. No face is visible.

REVIEW LOG (made up)
  Round 1  maker: ad v1.
           reviewer, same chat as the maker: "Looks great. Approved."
  Round 1  (second try) separate reviewer, using draft 2:
           1 pass   2 pass   3 FAIL (the lid is brown in shot 4)   4 pass
  Round 2  maker: ad v2.
           separate reviewer: 1 pass   2 pass   3 pass   4 pass
  After the pass  the agent makes a last edit to shot 3.
  Delivery  The agent sends the edited v2 to the client. No review ran
           after the edit.

questions.prompt: Which line in the exhibit is gradeable by two different reviewers, with the same answer?

options.text: The ad feels premium, so that a viewer thinks the tea is a high-end product
options.explanation: Premium is a feeling. Two reviewers may disagree, and Claude's docs warn that vague criteria give noisy results.

options.text: Overall quality is high, which covers the picture, the sound and the story together
options.explanation: This covers too much to score. Claude's docs say each criterion is scored on its own.

options.text: The logo is readable in the last 2 seconds, which has a plain yes or no answer
options.explanation: Right. Claude's docs prefer explicit criteria, such as a column that holds numbers, over a vague line like "the data looks good".

options.text: The ad is on brand, since the agent already knows the brand better than a person does
options.explanation: On brand is a judgment, and a claim about the agent's knowledge is not a criterion at all.

questions.prompt: In Round 1, a reviewer in the same chat as the maker wrote "Looks great. Approved." What is the best fix?

options.text: Use a separate reviewer with its own context and the studio's rubric, as in the second try
options.explanation: Right. Claude's grader runs in a separate context window so the maker's choices do not influence it. In the log, the separate reviewer found the lid problem.

options.text: Ask the same chat to review again, and this time tell it to be much harsher
options.explanation: The same chat still carries the maker's context. A harsher tone does not give it a rubric.

options.text: Remove the review step, because a reviewer that approves a bad ad costs more than none
options.explanation: A reviewer with a clear rubric found a real fault. The step is worth keeping, with a better setup.

options.text: Let the maker's own review stand, because the maker knows the ad better than anyone
options.explanation: The maker's context is exactly what Claude's docs keep away from the grader.

questions.prompt: The reviewer found that the lid is brown in shot 4. What should it send back to the maker?

options.text: The words "Fail. Try again.", so that the maker has the freedom to find its own way
options.explanation: This tells the maker nothing. Claude's grader returns which criteria passed or failed.

options.text: A new full storyboard, with the lid problem hidden among ten other small suggestions
options.explanation: A pile of changes hides the one that matters, and risks breaking what already passes.

options.text: A score out of 10 for the ad, with no note on which line caused the lower score
options.explanation: A score without the failed line gives the maker nothing to change.

options.text: Line 3 failed: the lid is brown in shot 4, so keep the rest and make the lid green
options.explanation: Right. Name the failed line and the one change, like Google's "Keep everything the same, but change…" style of follow-up.

questions.prompt: Delivery: the agent sent v2 after a review that came before the last edit to shot 3. What is the problem?

options.text: No problem, because a pass stays true for any later version of the same ad
options.explanation: A pass describes the file that was checked. A later edit makes it a different file.

options.text: The check should have run on the final file, because the pass no longer describes v2
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's output check is on the final output, before it leaves the system. Here the final file was never checked.

options.text: The problem is that the reviewer was a model, and a model can never review an ad
options.explanation: A model reviewer is fine for rubric lines. The problem here is what was reviewed and when.

options.text: The ad should have gone to the client sooner, so the edit would never have been made
options.explanation: Speed is not the issue. The issue is that the delivered file was never checked.

questions.prompt: The client says: "Run a loop until it decides which of these two ads is more beautiful." What do you advise?

options.text: Agree, since a loop with a strong model can judge beauty as well as any person can
options.explanation: Anthropic says the pattern fits when there are clear evaluation criteria. Beauty has none here.

options.text: Write a rubric of 40 lines so that beauty is covered, and run the loop 20 times
options.explanation: More lines do not make taste gradeable. Forty vague lines are still vague.

options.text: Skip a loop, since nobody can write the criteria and a person picks the ad they prefer
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says an evaluator loop works with clear criteria and measurable gains. With none, a person chooses.

options.text: Run the loop only on the logo, and let the client pick the ad on the logo result alone
options.explanation: The question was about which ad is more beautiful. A logo check does not answer it.
